questions.domainName: Domain 1: Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity
questions.statement: A global conglomerate operates 300 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations with multiple nested Organizational Units (OUs). The central security team requires that all member account IAM users and roles be strictly prevented from creating unencrypted Amazon S3 buckets or disabling AWS CloudTrail in any AWS region, while allowing specific automated deployment pipelines in the Infrastructure OU to manage custom KMS key policies without disruption. Furthermore, the solution must prevent member account administrators (including root) from bypassing these controls. Which architecture enforces these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Apply Service Control Policies (SCPs) with explicit Deny conditions at the intermediate OU levels for S3 encryption and CloudTrail protection, while applying a dedicated SCP to the Infrastructure OU that leaves KMS management permissions untouched.
options.explanation: Correct: SCPs establish guardrails across OUs without impacting accounts in sister OUs. Applying granular SCPs at intermediate OUs enforces preventive controls on member accounts (including root) without restricting KMS operations in the Infrastructure OU.

options.text: Attach a Service Control Policy (SCP) to the Root OU that explicitly denies s3:CreateBucket without encryption headers and cloudtrail:StopLogging/DeleteTrail, excluding the Infrastructure OU by placing it outside the Root hierarchy.
options.explanation: Incorrect: All accounts and OUs in AWS Organizations must reside under the Root container; an OU cannot be placed outside the Root.

options.text: Deploy IAM Permission Boundaries on every IAM role in all 300 accounts using AWS Systems Manager Automation runbooks, and schedule daily compliance scans with AWS Config.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Permission boundaries do not apply to the root user in member accounts and require massive ongoing maintenance compared to declarative SCPs.

options.text: Deploy AWS CloudFormation StackSets across all accounts to provision IAM Deny policies and configure AWS WAF on all regional endpoints.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Member account administrators can modify or delete IAM policies created by CloudFormation StackSets, failing the requirement to prevent bypass.

questions.generalExplanation: Service Control Policies (SCPs) in AWS Organizations enforce guardrails that apply to all principals (including the account root user) in member accounts without modifying individual IAM policies.

questions.domainName: Domain 1: Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity
questions.statement: An enterprise with 50 VPCs across multiple AWS accounts uses an AWS Transit Gateway for inter-VPC and internet connectivity. The security architecture mandates that all east-west (inter-VPC) and north-south (outbound internet) traffic must pass through a centralized inspection VPC containing stateful AWS Network Firewall appliances. During initial testing, TCP sessions between VPCs are intermittently dropping due to asymmetric routing across Availability Zones. How should the network architect resolve this issue?

options.text: Enable Transit Gateway Appliance Mode on the VPC attachment for the Inspection VPC in all Availability Zones.
options.explanation: Correct: Enabling Appliance Mode on the Transit Gateway VPC attachment ensures bidirectional traffic within a flow is routed through the same Availability Zone and Elastic Network Interface (ENI), preventing asymmetric routing through stateful firewalls.

options.text: Configure Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing on the Transit Gateway route tables with a maximum path limit of 1.
options.explanation: Incorrect: ECMP operates at BGP/Direct Connect layer and does not guarantee AZ symmetry for VPC attachments.

options.text: Replace the AWS Network Firewall with an Application Load Balancer in each spoke VPC.
options.explanation: Incorrect: ALBs cannot inspect non-HTTP traffic or handle general east-west Layer 3/4 packet inspection.

options.text: Deploy a mesh of VPC Peering connections between all 50 VPCs and route traffic directly.
options.explanation: Incorrect: VPC peering creates exponential complexity (N*(N-1)/2) and bypasses the centralized inspection VPC.

questions.generalExplanation: Transit Gateway Appliance Mode guarantees that symmetric traffic flows for a given network session are directed to the same Availability Zone where the stateful firewall resides.

questions.domainName: Domain 1: Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity
questions.statement: A multinational enterprise wants to simplify VPC network management across 80 development accounts. The network team wants to centrally manage subnets, route tables, and NAT Gateways in a dedicated Network Hub account, while allowing developers in member accounts to launch EC2 instances and ECS tasks inside shared private subnets without having administrative control over the underlying network configuration. Which solution achieves this with the LEAST operational complexity?

options.text: Use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share subnets from the centralized VPC in the Network Hub account with the AWS Organization or specific OUs.
options.explanation: Correct: VPC Sharing via AWS RAM allows central network ownership while participant accounts can launch compute resources into shared subnets without modifying networking constructs.

options.text: Create VPCs in each member account and establish AWS Transit Gateway VPC attachments to the central Network Hub account.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Creating individual VPCs in 80 accounts multiplies VPC management, CIDR allocation, and NAT Gateway infrastructure costs.

options.text: Configure an AWS CloudFormation template that deploys identical VPCs and IAM roles across all accounts, syncing routes via AWS Lambda.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Custom Lambda synchronization adds high failure risk and does not provide unified network ownership.

options.text: Create VPC Peering between the Network Hub account and all 80 member accounts with DNS resolution enabled.
options.explanation: Incorrect: VPC Peering does not allow participants to share subnets directly and requires managing 80 individual peering connections.

questions.generalExplanation: VPC sharing (via AWS RAM) enables multiple AWS accounts to create application resources (EC2, ECS, RDS) in centrally managed, shared VPC subnets within an organization.

questions.domainName: Domain 1: Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity
questions.statement: A financial institution has two 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect dedicated connections terminating at two different Direct Connect locations for high resiliency. The on-premises data center needs to connect to 120 VPCs across 4 AWS Regions. The architecture requires active/passive BGP routing over the AWS global network with automatic failover, MACsec encryption over the dedicated interconnects, and minimal BGP peer management overhead. Which combination of services should the architect deploy?

options.text: Create Private Virtual Interfaces (Private VIFs) directly from the Direct Connect connections to each of the 120 VPCs across all 4 regions.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Direct Connect connections support a maximum of 50 Private VIFs and do not scale to 120 VPCs across multiple regions without a Direct Connect Gateway.

options.text: Deploy IPsec VPN tunnels over the public internet to each VPC and terminate them on virtual private gateways.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Standard IPsec VPNs have a 1.25 Gbps bandwidth limit and do not utilize the 10 Gbps dedicated Direct Connect infrastructure.

options.text: Provision a Direct Connect Gateway, associate it with regional AWS Transit Gateways in each AWS Region via Transit Virtual Interfaces (Transit VIFs), enable MACsec on Direct Connect ports, and use BGP AS-Path prepending for failover.
options.explanation: Correct: Direct Connect Gateway with Transit VIFs connected to regional Transit Gateways scales to hundreds of VPCs across regions, supports MACsec on 10G/100G dedicated links, and uses BGP AS-Path prepending for active/passive path selection.

options.text: Attach Direct Connect connections directly to an AWS Network Load Balancer in each region.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Direct Connect connects at Layer 2/3 via VIFs and Direct Connect Gateways, not directly to NLBs.

questions.generalExplanation: Using a Direct Connect Gateway with Transit VIFs attached to regional AWS Transit Gateways enables scalable multi-VPC multi-region hybrid connectivity with hardware-level MACsec encryption.

questions.statement: An analytics service running in Account A needs to read encrypted customer datasets from an Amazon S3 bucket located in Account B. The objects in Account B are encrypted with an AWS KMS Customer Managed Key (CMK) located in Account B. What configuration is required to grant the IAM role in Account A permission to decrypt and read the S3 objects?

options.text: Export the KMS private key from Account B and import it into an AWS KMS key in Account A.
options.explanation: Incorrect: KMS Customer Managed Keys are non-exportable; AWS KMS manages symmetric key material inside HSMs.

options.text: Change the encryption on the S3 bucket in Account B to AWS Managed Key (aws/s3), which automatically permits all cross-account IAM roles.
options.explanation: Incorrect: The default AWS Managed Key (aws/s3) cannot be shared across different AWS accounts; cross-account KMS requires Customer Managed Keys.

options.text: Configure an S3 ACL on the Account B bucket granting public read permissions.
options.explanation: Incorrect: ACLs do not grant KMS decryption permissions and making the bucket public creates massive security exposure.

options.text: Attach an IAM policy to the role in Account A granting kms:Decrypt and s3:GetObject, configure the S3 bucket policy in Account B to allow the Account A role ARN, and update the KMS Key Policy in Account B to allow the Account A role ARN (or Account A root) to perform kms:Decrypt.
options.explanation: Correct: Cross-account KMS and S3 access requires explicit delegation: the IAM identity policy in Account A, the S3 bucket resource policy in Account B, and the KMS Key Policy in Account B must all permit the action.

questions.statement: An enterprise uses AWS Control Tower to govern its multi-account environment. The security governance team requires a custom detective guardrail to ensure that no Amazon EBS volume is created without an 'Owner' tag and that non-compliant volumes are flagged across all existing and newly provisioned accounts automatically. How should this be implemented?

options.text: Deploy an Amazon CloudWatch scheduled rule on an EC2 instance in the management account to query the AWS Cost and Usage Report.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Cost and Usage Reports have hours of billing latency and cannot evaluate real-time resource tagging compliance.

options.text: Manually create an AWS Config rule in each account via the AWS Management Console whenever a new account is enrolled.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Manual creation is error-prone, unscalable, and does not apply automatically to future accounts.

options.text: Deploy a custom AWS Config Rule across the organization using Customizations for AWS Control Tower (CfCT) or AWS Control Tower Custom Controls (governance guardrails).
options.explanation: Correct: Customizations for AWS Control Tower (CfCT) or native Control Tower custom guardrails enable deployment of custom AWS Config rules and CloudFormation templates across all accounts automatically.

options.text: Attach a Service Control Policy (SCP) to the root OU that explicitly denies ec2:CreateVolume without an Owner tag.
options.explanation: Incorrect: SCPs are preventive controls (blocking creation), whereas the requirement specifically asks for a detective guardrail that flags non-compliant existing resources.

questions.generalExplanation: Customizations for AWS Control Tower (CfCT) allows customers to deploy custom preventive and detective guardrails (AWS Config rules) across all accounts managed by Control Tower.

questions.statement: A fintech company is designing a globally distributed payment processing platform deployed across us-east-1 (Primary) and eu-west-1 (Secondary). The database layer requires relational ACID compliance, sub-second cross-region replication lag, and the capability to perform unplanned disaster recovery failover in under 1 minute with zero data loss (RPO = 0 or near 0). Which database architecture meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables with multi-region active-active replication.
options.explanation: Incorrect: DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value store, not a relational ACID SQL database as required.

options.text: Amazon Aurora Global Database with the primary cluster in us-east-1 and a secondary cluster in eu-west-1, utilizing dedicated storage-level replication and fast cross-region failover.
options.explanation: Correct: Amazon Aurora Global Database replicates storage blocks across regions in typically under 1 second without impacting compute performance, and supports managed planned/unplanned failover in under 1 minute.

options.text: Amazon Redshift Multi-Region cluster with streaming data ingestion.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Amazon Redshift is an analytical data warehouse, not a transactional OLTP payment engine.

options.text: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ with an asynchronous cross-region read replica in eu-west-1.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Standard RDS cross-region read replicas use asynchronous replication with higher lag (seconds to minutes) and require manual promotion and reconfiguration.

questions.generalExplanation: Amazon Aurora Global Database uses dedicated storage hardware to replicate data across AWS Regions with typical latency of under 1 second, providing fast cross-region disaster recovery for relational workloads.

questions.statement: An e-commerce order ingestion pipeline receives 20,000 orders per second during flash sales. The system must guarantee that orders for the same customer account are processed strictly in chronological sequence, duplicate orders are filtered out, and failed orders are isolated without blocking other customers' orders. Which serverless architecture satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Amazon SQS Standard queue with maximum visibility timeout, polled by an EC2 Auto Scaling group running single-threaded Python scripts.
options.explanation: Incorrect: SQS Standard queues provide at-least-once delivery and do not guarantee strict message ordering.

options.text: Amazon SQS FIFO queue configured with customer ID as the Message Group ID, content-based deduplication enabled, backed by an AWS Lambda consumer with a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) configured.
options.explanation: Correct: SQS FIFO with Message Group ID guarantees strict ordering per customer while allowing high concurrent parallel processing across different customers. Content-based deduplication prevents duplicates and a DLQ isolates failed messages.

options.text: Amazon SNS Standard topic broadcasting to 10 AWS Lambda functions in parallel.
options.explanation: Incorrect: SNS Standard does not guarantee ordering or automatic message deduplication.

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose writing directly to Amazon S3 with an Athena table partitioned by customer ID.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Kinesis Firehose buffers in batches and is designed for analytics delivery, not low-latency transactional order processing.

questions.generalExplanation: Amazon SQS FIFO queues with Message Group IDs provide per-group strict ordering, deduplication, and dead-letter queue isolation for mission-critical transactional pipelines.

options.text: AWS Step Functions Express Workflows with maximum timeout of 5 minutes.

options.text: Chaining AWS Lambda functions synchronously where each function calls the next function via the AWS SDK.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Lambda functions have a 15-minute maximum timeout and synchronous chaining cannot wait 3 days for human review.

questions.generalExplanation: AWS Step Functions Standard Workflows are designed for long-running workflows (up to 1 year) and provide native callback tokens (Task Tokens) for asynchronous human approvals.

questions.statement: A global news network delivers live breaking news videos and articles. During major world events, viewer traffic spikes by 1,000x within 30 seconds. The solution must cache dynamic API responses and static assets at edge locations, execute sub-millisecond edge compute logic to personalize HTTP headers based on viewer country, and protect the origin servers from request collapse. Which combination of services should the architect recommend?

options.text: Deploy an Application Load Balancer in each AWS Region and use Amazon Route 53 Geolocation routing with no edge caching.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Without edge caching, sudden 1,000x traffic surges will hit the backend origins directly, leading to resource exhaustion.

options.text: Use AWS Global Accelerator with EC2 instances running NGINX caching reverse proxies.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Global Accelerator optimizes network routing but does not provide HTTP edge caching, Origin Shield, or serverless edge compute.

options.text: Deploy Amazon CloudFront with CloudFront Functions for edge header manipulation, configure Origin Shield and cache policies, and attach AWS WAF to the distribution.
options.explanation: Correct: CloudFront Functions provide ultra-low-latency (<1ms) edge header modification, CloudFront Origin Shield eliminates redundant requests to protect origin servers during traffic surges, and AWS WAF provides edge security.

options.text: Configure Amazon API Gateway with Lambda Authorizers and disable CloudFront distribution.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Disabling CloudFront removes global edge caching and exposes backend Lambdas to massive concurrency spikes.

questions.generalExplanation: Amazon CloudFront with CloudFront Functions and Origin Shield minimizes origin load during extreme traffic surges while personalizing requests at the edge in sub-milliseconds.

options.text: Store application configuration feature flags in AWS Secrets Manager and schedule automatic secret rotation.

options.text: Store configuration JSON files in an Amazon S3 bucket with versioning and S3 Event Notifications configured.

options.explanation: Correct: AWS AppConfig enables teams to create, validate, deploy, and monitor application configurations with custom deployment strategies (linear/canary) and automated CloudWatch alarm rollback.

options.text: Use Oracle Data Pump to export dump files to S3, and write custom Python scripts to convert PL/SQL to PL/pgSQL.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Custom scripting of database procedures is error-prone, and Data Pump export creates high downtime during cutover.

options.text: Use AWS DataSync to copy Oracle raw database datafiles directly into an Aurora PostgreSQL EBS volume.
options.explanation: Incorrect: DataSync cannot convert heterogeneous database data formats (Oracle proprietary binary blocks cannot be read directly by PostgreSQL engine).

options.text: Deploy AWS Application Migration Service (AWS MGN) to replicate the Oracle server directly to an Amazon EC2 instance running PostgreSQL.
options.explanation: Incorrect: AWS MGN is a block-level server migration tool and does not convert database schemas across heterogeneous database engines.

options.text: Use AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to convert the Oracle database schema, stored procedures, and triggers to PostgreSQL, then use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with Full Load and Change Data Capture (CDC) to synchronize data continuously until cutover.
options.explanation: Correct: AWS SCT converts heterogeneous database schemas and code (Oracle to PostgreSQL), while AWS DMS performs initial full load and continuous CDC replication to keep data synchronized until cutover.

questions.generalExplanation: Heterogeneous database migrations require AWS SCT (to convert schemas, views, and stored procedures) combined with AWS DMS (to replicate historical data and stream ongoing CDC changes).

options.text: Mount the on-premises NAS on an EC2 instance and run the `aws s3 sync` CLI command over a cron job.

options.text: Deploy an AWS DataSync agent on-premises and configure a DataSync task with bandwidth throttling and verification enabled to transfer data directly from the NAS to Amazon S3.
options.explanation: Correct: AWS DataSync is purpose-built for high-speed automated file transfers from on-prem NAS/NFS systems to S3, preserving POSIX metadata and performing automated end-to-end data integrity validation.
